text: Doyle–Kirmse Reaction of S-Allyl and S-Propargyl Phosphorothioates
Laurine Tual<sup>◊</sup> Charlou Rognan<sup>◊</sup> Timothé Maujean<sup>◊</sup> Romain Pertschi Nicolas Girard Gaëlle Blond Mihaela Gulea\* 0-2
Université de Strasbourg, CNRS, Laboratoire d’Innovation Thérapeutique, LIT UMR 7200, 67000 Strasbourg, France gulea@unistra.fr
Published as part of the Special Topic C–S Bond Forming and Cleaving Reactions
Published online: 11.01.2025 (Accepted Manuscript), 25.02.2025 (Version of Record) DOI: 10.1055/a-2515-0351; Art ID: SS-2024-11-0461-OP

Abstract The Doyle–Kirmse reaction represents a powerful synthetic tool for forming both C–S and C–C bonds in a single process. The rhodium-catalyzed Doyle–Kirmse reaction of S-allyl and S-propargyl phosphorothioates with diazoesters has been developed and represents a rare example involving substrates bearing an electron-withdrawing group on the sulfur atom. The transformation takes place at room temperature, in only 5 minutes, and leads via a [2,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement of the sulfonium ylide intermediate to the corresponding S-homoallyl or S-homoallenyl phosphorothioates in yields ranging from 25% to 92% (19 examples).
Key words Doyle–Kirmse reaction, [2,3]-rearrangement, propargyl sulfides, allyl sulfides, diazoesters, phosphorothioates, C–S bond formation

The Doyle–Kirmse reaction is a powerful method for forming both C–S and C–C bonds in a single process, enabling the synthesis of a wide range of homoallyl or homoallenyl sulfides.<sup>1</sup> The metal-catalyzed version consists of the reaction of an allyl or a propargyl sulfide and a metal carbene species classically generated by the decomposition of a diazo compound (Scheme 1, A). This leads to the key intermediate of this reaction which is a sulfonium ylide that can be either metal-bound or metal-free depending mainly on the nature of the substrate and metal. The resulting ylide can then evolve through a [2,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement to the corresponding homoallyl or homoallenyl sulfide. Various transition-metal complexes, mainly based on rhodium and copper, but also on ruthenium, iron, cobalt, silver, platinum and gold, have been used in this reaction. The use of chiral metal complexes made possible enantioselective versions of the reaction.<sup>1g</sup> More recent research described a metal-free Doyle–Kirmse reaction using light-mediated diazo decomposition that generates free carbene species.<sup>1h,i</sup> A literature survey revealed that among the different substrates used in this reaction, aryl and alkyl sulfides represent the overwhelming majority, while derivatives bearing an electron-withdrawing group (EWG) on the sulfur have been sparsely reported (Scheme 1, A). This may be due to the concern that the sulfur, depleted by an electron-withdrawing substituent, would be less reactive toward the electrophilic metal carbene species. However, allyl and propargyl trifluoromethyl sulfides were successfully used in enantioselective Doyle–Kirmse reactions employing chiral rhodium or copper complexes (Scheme 1, B).<sup>2</sup> Another example, that we recently reported, concerned propargyl thiocyanates (Scheme 1, C).<sup>3</sup> In this case, the products were not isolated, as they subsequently rearranged to the isothiocyanate derivatives via a thio-Claisen reaction. Interestingly, when S-allyl or S-propargyl thioacetates were reacted with aryl diazoketones, the S-ylide formation was followed by sulfur-to-oxygen acyl transfer, and not by the [2,3]-rearrangement, thus leading to alkenyl sulfides instead of the expected products (Scheme 1, D).<sup>4</sup>
These literature data prompted us to investigate the reactivity of S-allyl and S-propargyl phosphorothioates, as new electron-poor sulfide substrates, toward -diazocarbonyl compounds.

Moreover, the phosphorothioates, which belong to the class of P(V) organophosphorus compounds,<sup>5</sup> have found important applications as biologically active molecules in agrochemical and pharmaceutical fields.<sup>6</sup> Their preparation, as well as their uses as synthetic intermediates in various transformations, most of which involving the cleavage of the P–S or C–S bond, have been independently reviewed in 2018 by O’Sullivan and co-workers, and by our group.<sup>7</sup> Two other reviews that followed dealt with modern methods to access phosphorothioates by phosphorus–sulfur bond formation and by direct phosphorothiolation reactions, respectively.<sup>8</sup> A recently reported synthesis of phos-

The reaction of a phosphorothioate with the metallocarbene resulting from diazo compound decomposition would, in the first step, lead to a phosphoryl sulfonium ylide which, to our knowledge, is still an unknown species. The so-formed S-ylide can then evolve along three possible pathways: [2,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement yielding the Doyle–Kirmse reaction product I, S-to-O phosphoryl transfer (similar to the acyl transfer), leading to the alkenyl phosphate II, or S-to-C phosphoryl group migration,<sup>10</sup> resulting in the -sulfanyl phosphonate III (Scheme 1, E). Herein, we describe the rhodium-catalyzed reaction of S-allyl and Spropargyl phosphorothioates with diazoesters, leading exclusively to the Doyle–Kirmse [2,3]-rearrangement products I.

To set up the reaction conditions, easily available O,Odiisopropyl S-propargyl phosphorothioate (1a) was selected as a model substrate. Initial experiments were performed by adding 2-diazo-2-phenylacetate 3a (1.5 equiv) to a solution of 1a (1.0 equiv) in toluene $( c = 0 . 1 \mathrm { \sf ~ M } )$ , in the presence of $\mathtt { R h } _ { 2 } ( \mathrm { O A c } ) _ { 4 }$ (1 mol%) as a catalyst, to ensure effective diazo decomposition to generate rhodium carbene (Table 1, entry 1). After only 10 minutes, <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectroscopic analysis of the crude mixture revealed full conversion of the diazo partner 3a and the expected homoallenyl phosphorothioate 4aa was identified as the major product of a complex crude reaction mixture (31%, <sup>1</sup>H NMR yield) and was isolated in 31% yield. With this result in hand, optimization studies were conducted further. First, the nature of the ligand on the rhodium dimer catalyst was investigated, switching from acetate (OAc) to the bulky pivalate (OPiv) or to the electro-deficient trifluoroacetate (TFA). The use of the first complex led to a higher conversion compared to the acetate, however a lower <sup>1</sup>H NMR yield was measured (entry 2 vs 1), while the second complex led to a lower conversion and yield (entry 3 vs 1). We selected the $\mathtt { R h _ { 2 } ( O A c ) _ { 4 } }$ for further experiments, as it represented the best compromise between conversion and yield. Then, the influence of the number of equivalents of diazoester part ner 3a was investigated in an attempt to increase the conversion of 1a to completion. Indeed, increasing from 1.5 to 2.0 equivalents of 3a substantially improved conversion and yield (entry 1 vs 4 and 5). With 4.0 equivalents full conversion (>99%) of the starting phosphorothioate 1a was reached and 4aa was obtained in 70% yield (entry 6). To further improve the yield of the transformation, the impact of the solvent was investigated. To our surprise, a switch from toluene to dichloromethane was detrimental to the reaction as only 12% of 4aa was actually obtained and a fast decomposition and dimerization of the diazo partner was observed (entry 7). Dichloroethane (DCE) was then tested and resulted in a smooth diazo decomposition with full conversion (>99%) of the starting material 1a, leading to 4aa in a good isolated yield of 85% (entry 8). It is worth noting that the use of DCE also reduced the reaction time from 10 minutes to 5 minutes. When lowering the catalytic charge to only 0.1 mol%, the reaction was still efficient, with a conversion of 98% and an NMR yield of 80% (entry 9). The nature of the metal catalyst was also investigated by testing the ruthenium(II) complex $[ ( \eta ^ { 6 } { - } C _ { 6 } \mathrm { H } _ { 6 } ) \mathrm { R u C l } ( \mu { - } \mathrm { C l } ) ] _ { 2 } ,$ copper thiophene-2-carboxylate, silver triflate and palladium(II) chloride, but in all cases no conversion of the starting material 1a was observed (Table 1, entries 10–13). In the case of the Ru, Ag and Pd catalysts, diazoester decomposition occurred and led to dimerization of the carbene, while with CuTC the diazoester was recovered. Finally, we kept the reaction conditions given in entry 8 for our further experiments.

With these optimal conditions in hand, several structural modifications of the reaction partners were investigated to explore the scope and limitations of the transformation (Scheme 2). Changing the isopropyl groups on the phosphoryl of 1 to ethyl or L-menthyl groups did not change the reactivity, leading to similar yields. Unfortunately, the asymmetric Doyle–Kirmse reaction using dimenthyl phosphorothioate 1c as the chiral substrate was not diastereoselective, leading to a very low diastereomeric ratio of 58:42. The chiral substrate 1c was also reacted using a chiral Rh(II) catalyst derived from (S)-N-naphthalene-2,3-dicarboxyl-tert-leucine $\begin{array} { r } { [ \mathrm { R h } _ { 2 } ( S \mathrm { - B P T T L } ) _ { 4 } ] , ^ { 1 1 } } \end{array}$ but the diastereomeric ratio and the NMR yield of the product 4ca remained the same. This indicates that no chiral information was transferred from the metal complex to the substrate, suggesting that the rearrangement occurs via an ylide-free pathway.

text: Next, the structure of the propargyl moiety was modified. We prepared substrates 1d–f bearing an ethyl, a cyclopropyl or a phenyl substituent, respectively, on the triple bond. They were reacted with diazoester 3a under the standard reaction conditions, and all of them were successfully transformed into the desired products 4. Ethyl and cyclopropyl derivatives 4da and 4ea were isolated in very good yields of 92% and 85%, respectively, whereas phenyl derivative 4fa was obtained in 62% yield.

Modification of the substituent on the aryl group of the diazo derivative was then considered. Using methyl 2-aryl-2-diazoacetates $\mathbf { 3 6 - g }$ in reactions with phosphorothioate 1a, the desired homoallenyl phosphorothioates 4 were obtained, regardless of the position or electronic nature of the substituent on the aromatic ring. The only exception was the 4-OMe derivative 3h, which decomposed and dimerized, leaving substrate 1a intact. The use of diazoesters 3d–f with an electron-withdrawing group such as $\mathrm { C F } _ { 3 }$ and ${ \Nu } 0 _ { 2 }$ reduced the efficiency of the reaction leading to lower yields (25% to 46%), which may be attributed to the increased electrophilicity and reactivity of the corresponding metal carbenes. The L-menthyl diazoacetate 3i allowed us to obtain product 4ai in 56% yield and a diastereoselectivity of 66:34. Acceptor–acceptor diazo derivatives such as dimethyl diazomalonate or acetyl diazoacetate proved to be ineffective, as the expected homoallenyl phosphorothioates 4aj and 4ak were not observed.

We then examined the efficiency of the reaction in the S-allyl series, by using different phosphorothioates 2a–f and the diazoester partner 3a. Starting from substrate 2a, the S-homoallyl derivative 5aa was obtained in a good yield of 83%. When S-crotyl 2b (77:23 ratio of E/Z-isomers) and S-cinnamyl phosphorothioates 2c (100% E-isomer) were used, slightly lower yields were reached, 65% for 5ba and 50% for 5ca. In both cases, no diastereoselectivity was observed, and products 5ba and 5ca were obtained as mixtures of diastereomers in \~1:1 ratio. On the other hand, Sdimethylhomoallyl phosphorothioate 5da was obtained in a good yield of 82% from the S-prenyl precursor 2d, without any detection of deprenylated byproducts in the crude reaction mixture, as previously reported for the phenyl sulfide series.<sup>12</sup> The S-methallyl 2e and S-bromoallyl 2f substrates also led to the corresponding S-homoallyl phosphorothioates, in 44% and 67% yield, respectively.

To showcase the robustness and practicality of our method, the reaction was scaled up to 1 mmol of sulfide 1a and 4 mmol of diazoester 3a, using only 0.1 mol% of Rh catalyst. In this case, 20 minutes was necessary for a complete conversion and phosphorothioate 4aa was isolated in 64% yield.

Taking advantage of the presence of the carboxylate and the double bond functionalities in the obtained products, we engaged an S-homoallyl phosphorothioate in an intramolecular Brønsted acid catalyzed hydroacyloxylation to access a lactone. By treating phosphorothioate 5ea with 1 equivalent of p-toluenesulfonic acid (PTSA) monohydrate, 5-exo-trig cyclization was achieved efficiently, leading to the expected lactone 6ea in 62% yield (Scheme 3).

text: In summary, we have developed a rhodium-catalyzed Doyle–Kirmse reaction of S-allyl and S-propargyl phosphorothioates with aryl diazoacetates. This represents a rare example of Doyle–Kirmse reaction involving derivatives bearing an electron-withdrawing group on sulfur. The transformation occurs under mild conditions, at room temperature, in only 5 minutes, and exhibits a good substrate tolerance. It led via the [2,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement of sulfonium ylides to various S-homoallyl and S-homoallenyl phosphorothioates (19 examples) in yields ranging from 25% to 92%. To illustrate the potential post-functionalization of the obtained products, a phosphorothioate-substituted lactone was prepared by acid-catalyzed cyclization of the carboxylate function onto the homoallyl double bond.

From an organic synthesis point of view, this reaction is a practical method toward accessing a series of compounds containing a quaternary carbon stereocenter bearing a phosphorothioate functional group, which is of interest in drug design, and as a route to introduce P and/or S into molecules.

All reagents, chemicals and anhydrous solvents were purchased from commercial sources and used without purification. Reactions were monitored by TLC using Merck silica gel 60 F254 on aluminum sheets. TLC plates were visualized under UV light and revealed with acidic panisaldehyde stain or vanillin stain. Products were purified by flash column chromatography on Merck silica gel 60 (40–63 m) for normal phase or C18 for reverse phase. NMR spectra were recorded in CDCl on a Bruker spectrometer at 400 MHz for <sup>1</sup>H, at 101 MHz for <sup>13</sup>C, at 162 MHz for <sup>31</sup>P and at 376 MHz for ${ } ^ { 1 9 } \mathrm { F } .$ Proton-decoupled fluorine and phosphorus NMR spectra, <sup>19</sup>F{<sup>1</sup>H} NMR and <sup>31</sup>P{<sup>1</sup>H} NMR, were performed for all fluorinated and phosphorylated compounds. Proton chemical shifts are reported in ppm (), relative to residual $\mathrm { C H C l } _ { 3 }$ ( 7.26 ppm). Multiplicities are reported as follows: singlet (s), doublet (d), triplet (t), quartet (q), heptet (hept), multiplet (m) and combinations thereof. Coupling constant values J are given in Hz. Carbon chemical shifts are reported in ppm (), relative to the internal standard $\mathrm { C D C l } _ { 3 }$ ( 77.23 ppm). <sup>1</sup>H and $^ { 1 3 } \mathsf { C }$ NMR signals were assigned mostly on the basis of 2D-NMR (COSY, HSQC, HMBC) experiments. Diastereomeric ratios were determined according to <sup>1</sup>H NMR of the crude and NMR yields were determined using caffeine as internal standard in <sup>1</sup>H NMR. High-resolution mass spectral analyses were performed using an Agilent 1200 RRLC HPLC chain and an Agilent 6520 Accurate-Mass Q-ToF system.

The reaction mixture was then stirred at room temperature until completion, and the solvent was removed under vacuum. The crude was purified by flash chromatography on silica gel (n-pentane/Et O) to get pure product 4 or 5. A second purification using reverse-phase chromatography was performed for some examples difficult to purify on silica gel.
